one_liner: Batched SHA-256 of many fixed 64-byte inputs for Merkle trees; ~4.7x OpenSSL's per-message SHA256() on AVX2.
what_it_does: Hashes a layer of a binary Merkle tree: you pass a buffer of `count` 64-byte chunks (two 32-byte child nodes each) and get `count` 32-byte SHA-256 digests back, each identical to SHA256() of that 64-byte chunk. The C API is one call, `hashtree_hash(out, in, count)`, which dispatches on the CPU at runtime (optionally pinned with `hashtree_init`), plus directly callable per-ISA kernels. There is no streaming or arbitrary-length interface. Go (`Hash([][32]byte pairs)`, `HashByteSlice`), Rust (`hashtree-rs`) and Nim (`hashtree_abi`) bindings ship in the same repo.
how_it_is_fast: Multi-buffer SHA-256, taken from Intel's intel-ipsec-mb: 4, 8 or 16 independent messages are transposed into SIMD lanes (SSE/AVX x4, AVX2 x8, AVX-512 x16, NEON x4) and compressed together. On SHA-NI hardware it uses a 2-way interleaved SHA-NI kernel instead. Because every input is exactly 64 bytes, the second (padding) block is constant, so its message schedule is precomputed and stored as K+W constants (the `P`/`.LPADDING` tables), which skips that schedule on every hash. Kernels hand leftover blocks to the next narrower kernel (x16 to x8 to x4).
when_to_use: Merkleizing large SSZ or Ethereum beacon-state trees, or any binary Merkle tree whose nodes are 32 bytes, when you can hand over a whole layer per call

x86-64 CPUs without SHA-NI but with AVX2 or AVX-512: the README measures about 4.7x over per-message OpenSSL SHA256() with AVX2 x8, and about 12x over its own single-block kernel with AVX-512 x16 on Cascade Lake
Throughput-bound batch hashing of thousands of 64-byte records where results must be byte-identical to standard SHA-256
RISC-V boards with Zbb, where the README shows about 4.25x over the system OpenSSL for 64-byte messages
Go, Rust or Nim codebases that need a vetted SHA-256 Merkle hasher; Prysm (behind its --enable-hashtree flag) and status-im/nim-ssz-serialization already consume it
when_not_to_use: Messages that are not exactly 64 bytes, or streaming or incremental hashing: there is no such API, so use OpenSSL or ISA-L
Hashing one pair at a time (naive recursive Merkleization): the single-block kernels run at OpenSSL speed, and the author says one-at-a-time use is 'essentially the same as openssl's'
SHA-NI CPUs where you expect a large gain over OpenSSL: the README gives no same-run OpenSSL number there, and OpenSSL also uses SHA-NI
Raspberry Pi 4 class NEON-only ARM: the x4 NEON kernel is only 27% faster than its x1 kernel, with no OpenSSL comparison
Settings that need audited crypto: the maintainer closed the audit request as won't-fix, and the only assurance cited is differential fuzzing (EF, Prysm, and the nim-ssz-serialization fuzz target)

integration.form: static lib (libhashtree.a plus hashtree.h, with pkg-config and `make install`); also a Go module with prebuilt .syso objects, the Rust crate hashtree-rs (builds the C library via make), and the Nim package hashtree_abi
integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond stdint.h; cpuid.h on x86-64 builds; libm for benchmarks; optional OpenSSL (-lcrypto) for tests and benchmarks; the Go bindings need klauspost/cpuid/v2
integration.min_toolchain: A GCC/GNU-as compatible compiler; CI also builds with clang on Linux and with Apple clang's integrated assembler on macOS. Rust edition 2021, Nim >= 1.6.0, Go 1.21/1.22 in CI (go.mod says 1.22.2). Minimum GCC or binutils versions are not documented.
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSSE3/AVX/AVX2/AVX-512F+VL/SHA-NI kernels), aarch64 (NEON x1/x4 and SHA2-extension kernels, including Apple Silicon), riscv64 (base, Zbb, and Zknh+Zbkb kernels, selected via Linux riscv_hwprobe), and a scalar C fallback elsewhere; Linux, macOS and Windows (MinGW; benchmarks do not build on Windows)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The kernels only touch caller-supplied buffers, but the `hashtree_hash` dispatcher lazily writes a plain global function pointer on the first call without synchronization, so call `hashtree_init(NULL)` once before hashing from several threads.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the digests equal OpenSSL SHA256() for exactly-64-byte inputs, but the API is a batch call over fixed-size chunks, not SHA256()/EVP; callers must restructure Merkleization to pass whole layers

gotchas: No bounds checks: `in` must hold 64*count bytes and `out` 32*count bytes. The Rust `hash(out, chunks, count)` is a safe fn that does not check the slice lengths, so a wrong `count` is memory-unsafe from safe Rust. Its `init()` also declares a c_int return for a void C function, so the return value is meaningless.

Calling a named per-ISA kernel on a CPU without that ISA is undefined behavior (the header says so). Only `hashtree_hash` auto-detects, and on x86 it prefers SHA-NI x2 over AVX-512 x16 on purpose, because SHA-NI wins on small lists.

Toolchain fragility: v0.2.4 (PR #61) fixed wrong SHA results on the AArch64 path when built with Apple clang 21 (macOS 26.4). Issue #2 reported GNU as 2.39/2.40 looping forever on the asm macros. Prebuilt Go .syso objects triggered missing .note.GNU-stack linker warnings (issue #52, still open).

Go bindings: the assembly call cannot be preempted by the Go runtime, so before v0.2.6 (PR #71) one huge layer could stall every GC; calls are now capped at 2048 chunks. Open issue #48 reports erratic SHA-NI one-at-a-time timings on AMD.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Intel ISA-L Crypto's multi-buffer SHA when every input is a 64-byte node pair and you want one synchronous call with ARM/RISC-V kernels and Go/Rust/Nim bindings rather than a job-manager API for variable-length messages. Pick it over sha256mb or minio sha256-simd when you are outside Go or need AVX-512/SHA-NI paths, and over BLAKE3 when the protocol (e.g. Ethereum SSZ) mandates SHA-256.
verified_claims_summary: The README's bench.c hashes 75,000 random 64-byte messages (a 4.8 MB buffer). On an unnamed AVX2 x86-64 CPU without SHA-NI, the AVX2 x8 kernel in one call took 6.519 ms vs 30.519 ms for OpenSSL SHA256() called once per message (~4.7x). On a board labelled 'Banana Pi BPI-R3 with a RISC-V processor', the single-buffer Zbb kernel took 109.4 ms vs OpenSSL's 465.4 ms (~4.25x). Both runs were built with -O3 via src/Makefile, with no compiler or OpenSSL versions stated. The x86 gain is mostly multi-buffer vs single-buffer; the RISC-V gain is scalar (Zbb rotates plus the precomputed padding schedule). The Cascade Lake (~12x) and Go-vs-Prysm (~6-11x) figures are not against OpenSSL.
status_note: Active: v0.2.6 was tagged 2026-09-22 with RISC-V, Apple clang and Go-GC fixes through 2026; the code is MIT-licensed and vendorable (about 16 C/asm sources with no runtime dependencies), and Prysm now depends on its Go bindings (opt-in flag) while status-im's nim-ssz-serialization uses the Nim ABI.
